sentences.text: The Rodrigues starling was an extinct passerine bird belonging to the Sturnidae family, found only on Rodrigues Island within the Mascarene archipelago of the southwest Indian Ocean.
This species measured between 25 and 30 centimeters in length, a large size for a starling, and featured a long, robust beak.
Its plumage was white or whitish-grey, contrasting with dark brown wings, while its legs and beak were yellow.
Although the skull resembled that of the hoopoe starling in size, the overall skeleton was smaller.
The only known sighting of the living bird occurred when French sailor Julien Tafforet was marooned on the island between 1725 and 1726.
Historical accounts reveal the bird ate eggs and dead tortoises, tearing them apart with its powerful bill.
Descriptions from the past indicate the bird possessed a complex song.
Subfossil bones were first found by George Jenner in 1866 and 1871, followed by Henry H. Slater in 1874.
The genus Necropsar was formally named by Günther and Newton in 1879.
Robust limbs and strong jaws suggest the bird foraged for food on the ground.
It likely used its wedge-shaped bill to open entrances and remove objects while searching for food, supporting evidence that it consumed eggs and carrion.
Its diet may have included various snails and other invertebrates native to Rodrigues, as well as carrion.
Although capable of flight, the bird had a smaller sternum than other starlings, implying it did not need powerful flight due to the island's small size and topography.
Observations noted that pigeons and parrots from southern coastal islets visited the main island only for water, while breeding occurred on the islets because of rat persecution on the mainland.
The species was named Necropsar rodericanus, combining Greek words for 'dead' and 'starling' with the name of the island Rodrigues.
This species belongs to the genus Necropsar.
Günther and Newton considered the species likely identical to the bird described by Tafforet because of its strongly built bill.
In 1967, ornithologist James Greenway suggested the bird should belong to the same genus as the Réunion starling, Fregilupus, due to similarities between the two species.
However, in 1974, additional subfossils increased support for the hypothesis that the Rodrigues starling was a distinct genus.
It is debated whether the bird was sexually dimorphic due to insufficient fossil remains.
The Rodrigues starling was an extinct species endemic to the Mascarene island of Rodrigues.
It lived during the Holocene, from 0.0117 to 0 million years ago.
The species was extinct by the time of the 1761 French Transit of Venus expedition.
Tafforet observed that the bird lived on the islet of Gombrani located south of Rodrigues.
The Rodrigues starling went extinct on the mainland first, with Île Gombrani serving as its final refuge.
Masauji Hachisuka debated whether the subfossils described by Günther and Newton belonged to the bird reported by Tafforet, basing his argument on differences in diet and crest presence.
